opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that we're in this strange moment where we've built some of the most powerful technology in history, and we fundamentally don't understand how it works. We train these models by pouring in enormous amounts of data and compute, and out comes something that can write code, reason about science, and hold a conversation, but when you open it up, what you find is billions of numbers that nobody can read. We're essentially deploying black boxes into more and more critical parts of the economy and society.

That's uncomfortable for a few reasons. One is safety and reliability. If you don't understand why a model does what it does, you can't really guarantee it won't fail in some weird, unexpected way when it matters. Right now most of our tools for shaping model behavior are pretty blunt: you change the training data, you do some fine-tuning, you write a better prompt, and you hope it generalizes the way you want. It's a bit like trying to fix a car by only ever pressing the pedals differently and never opening the hood.

The second reason is control. Interpretability isn't just about looking inside the model and saying "oh, that's interesting." The really exciting part is that once you understand the internal representations, the concepts the model is actually using, you can start to intervene on them directly. You can find the feature responsible for some unwanted behavior and turn it down, or amplify something you want, in a much more precise and surgical way than retraining. That's what we mean by editing. It turns AI development from something closer to alchemy into something closer to engineering.

And the third reason, which I think people underappreciate, is discovery. These models are learning things about the world, in biology, in materials, in all kinds of scientific domains, that we may not know ourselves. If we can actually read out what they've learned, interpretability becomes a tool for generating new scientific knowledge, not just for auditing models.

So when I put all that together, I think understanding neural networks is one of the most important problems of this decade. If AI is going to be as transformative as many of us believe, we can't afford to keep treating it as a black box. We need to be able to understand it, debug it, and design it intentionally, and that's what Goodfire is trying to make possible.

r001.rationale: The response says understanding, editing, and debugging models can improve safety and reliability, and describes their deployment in critical parts of society and the economy.

r002.rationale: It presents access to internal representations as enabling precise interventions and intentional model design, contrasting that with simply training models from data and hoping for the desired behavior.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that we're building the most powerful technology in human history, and we fundamentally don't understand how it works. That's not a rhetorical flourish. If you ask the people training frontier models why a given model produced a given output, the honest answer is usually "we don't know." We can describe the training process, we can measure behavior on benchmarks, but the actual mechanism inside the network is a black box.

I think that's an untenable situation for a few reasons. The first is safety, obviously. If these systems are going to be making consequential decisions, in medicine, in infrastructure, in scientific research, we need to be able to look inside and verify that they're doing what we think they're doing, rather than just hoping the evals caught everything. Behavioral testing alone is like trying to understand a person by only watching what they do and never being able to ask why.

But the second reason, and the one I think is underappreciated, is that understanding is the path to control. Right now, the main lever we have for shaping model behavior is training: you gather data, you fine-tune, you run RLHF, and you hope the change generalizes the way you intended. It's slow, it's expensive, and it has side effects you often don't discover until later. Interpretability gives you a different kind of lever. If you can identify the internal features a model uses to represent a concept, you can read them to understand what the model is actually attending to, and you can write to them to change behavior directly and precisely. That's a qualitatively different relationship with the technology.

At Goodfire we think of neural networks as something more like a new kind of substrate that we're learning to engineer, rather than something you train and then hope for the best. Right now we're at a stage that's a bit like early biology before we had microscopes, or early computing before we had debuggers. Once you have the tools to see inside, the whole field changes. You go from alchemy to chemistry. And I think whoever develops those tools will shape how this technology gets deployed, which is why we see it as critical to build them now, while the systems are still legible enough that we have a real shot at it.

r001.rationale: The response says internal inspection and precise edits are needed to verify and control models used in consequential areas such as medicine and infrastructure, and compares interpretability tools to debuggers.

r002.rationale: It contrasts data gathering, fine-tuning, and RLHF with using internal features to change behavior directly, framing networks as a substrate to engineer intentionally.

astra-6.text:
I think the core issue is that we’re building increasingly powerful systems without really understanding how they work internally. We can train them, measure their performance, and observe their behavior, but that’s different from understanding how they arrive at a particular answer or why they fail.

Understanding what’s happening inside a neural network gives us a chance to move beyond trial and error. If we can identify the internal features driving a behavior, we can potentially intervene more precisely—preserving capabilities we want while changing behaviors we don’t.

That’s why I see understanding and editing as closely connected. Understanding gives us a basis for making changes, and editing lets us test whether that understanding is actually correct. As these systems become more capable and take on more consequential tasks, that ability to diagnose and deliberately shape their behavior becomes increasingly important.

r001.rationale: It connects understanding and editing to shaping behavior as systems take on consequential tasks, but it does not mention debugging or reliable deployment in mission-critical contexts.

r002.rationale: It describes probing internal features to guide deliberate changes, but does not contrast opening the black box with merely growing models from data or explicitly frame this as intentional model design.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’re entering a world where neural networks are becoming incredibly capable, but our ability to understand what’s happening inside them hasn’t kept pace. We can observe their behavior and train them to produce better answers, but that’s different from understanding how they arrive at those answers or why they fail.

At Goodfire, we see interpretability as a way to close that gap. If we can identify the concepts a model represents and understand how those concepts influence its behavior, we can start making more precise interventions. That could help us diagnose failures, steer models more reliably, and give people greater control over the systems they’re deploying.

The ambition is to turn neural networks into something we can understand and engineer with confidence. As these systems take on more consequential roles, that becomes increasingly important.

r001.rationale: It says interpretability can diagnose failures, enable more reliable steering, and give people greater control, and that understanding and engineering models with confidence becomes important as they take on consequential roles.

r002.rationale: It describes identifying represented concepts and intervening precisely to shape behavior, framing interpretability as a way to engineer models intentionally.
